title: Subarray Sums Divisible by K
description: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the number of non-empty contiguous subarrays whose sum is divisible by `k`.
hints: Track the running prefix sum modulo k, and count how many times each remainder has occurred.
Two prefixes with the same remainder mean the subarray between them is divisible by k.

title: Maximum Size Subarray Sum Equals k
description: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the length of the longest contiguous subarray that sums to exactly `k`, or `0` if none exists.
hints: Track the running prefix sum, and remember the FIRST index each prefix sum value occurred at.
A subarray ending at index i sums to k exactly when (prefix - k) was seen earlier — the earliest such occurrence gives the longest subarray.

title: Maximum Product of Three Numbers
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return the maximum product achievable by any three numbers in it.
hints: The best product is either the three largest numbers, or the two smallest (most negative) numbers times the single largest number.
Sort the array to easily access both ends.

title: Array Partition
description: Given an integer array `nums` of `2n` integers, group them into `n` pairs to maximize the sum of the minimum value in each pair. Return that maximized sum.
hints: Sort the array and pair up adjacent elements — the minimum of each pair is then just every element at an even index.

title: Rank Transform of an Array
description: Given an array of integers `arr`, replace every element with its rank (1-indexed, based on ascending sorted order, with equal elements getting the same rank). Return the resulting array.
hints: Sort the distinct values to determine each value's rank, then map every original element through that rank lookup.

title: Relative Sort Array
description: Given two arrays `arr1` and `arr2` where `arr2` contains distinct elements all present in `arr1`, sort `arr1` so its elements follow the same relative order as in `arr2`; elements not in `arr2` go at the end, sorted ascending.
constraints: All elements of arr2 are distinct and each appears in arr1.
hints: Sort arr1 using a custom key: elements present in arr2 sort by their position in arr2; elements absent sort after all of those, by their own value.

title: Height Checker
description: Students stand in a line with heights given by `heights`. Comparing to the array sorted in non-decreasing order, return the number of indices where the actual height differs from the expected (sorted) height.
hints: Sort a copy of the array and compare it position by position with the original, counting mismatches.

title: Sort Array by Increasing Frequency
description: Given an integer array `nums`, sort it in increasing order of frequency; if multiple values have the same frequency, sort those by decreasing value.
hints: Count the frequency of each value, then sort the array using a composite key of (frequency ascending, value descending).

title: K-diff Pairs in an Array
description: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the number of unique pairs `(x, y)` from `nums` such that `x - y == k` (`k >= 0`; a pair is counted once regardless of duplicate occurrences).
hints: Count occurrences of each value first.
If k == 0, count values that appear at least twice; otherwise, for each distinct value v, check whether v + k also exists.

title: Grumpy Bookstore Owner
description: Given `customers[i]` (customers entering during minute `i`) and `grumpy[i]` (1 if the owner is grumpy that minute, satisfied customers lost), the owner can use a special technique to stay not-grumpy for one contiguous window of `minutes` minutes. Return the maximum number of satisfied customers achievable.
hints: Start with the baseline satisfied count (every minute the owner isn't grumpy).
Slide a window of size `minutes` over the array, tracking how many ADDITIONAL customers (the grumpy-minute ones) would be saved by placing the technique there — maximize that extra gain.

title: Minimum Increment to Make Array Unique
description: Given an integer array `nums`, in one move you may increment any element by 1. Return the minimum number of moves so that every element is unique.
hints: Sort the array, then scan left to right: whenever the current element isn't strictly greater than the previous one, bump it up to (previous + 1), tracking the total increments made.

title: Where Will the Ball Fall
description: A grid `grid` of size `m x n` has diagonal walls: `1` for a board directing a ball to the bottom-right, `-1` for the bottom-left. Balls are dropped one per column at the top; a ball gets stuck if it hits a 'V' shape formed by boards or falls out of the grid's sides. Return an array giving, for each starting column, the column it ends up in (or `-1` if stuck).
hints: Simulate each ball independently, row by row: at each row, check the board direction and the board in the adjacent column it would move into — if they form a 'V' (opposite directions) or the ball would exit the grid, it gets stuck.

title: Sum of All Odd Length Subarrays
description: Given an array of positive integers `arr`, return the sum of all possible odd-length contiguous subarrays.
hints: For each index, count how many odd-length subarrays include it — that count times its value contributes to the total. This count can be derived from how many valid left/right boundary combinations exist, but brute force summation over every odd-length subarray is also simple and fine for this input size.

title: Find Pivot Index
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return the leftmost pivot index where the sum of all elements to its left equals the sum of all elements to its right (0 if no such elements on a side). Return `-1` if no pivot index exists.
hints: Track the total sum and a running left-side sum as you scan; at each index, the right-side sum is total - leftSum - nums[i]. Compare the two sides directly.

title: Kth Missing Positive Number
description: Given a strictly increasing array of positive integers `arr` and an integer `k`, return the `k`-th positive integer missing from `arr`.
hints: At index i (0-indexed), the number of missing positives before arr[i] is arr[i] - (i + 1). Binary search for the smallest index where that count is >= k.

title: Maximum Ascending Subarray Sum
description: Given an array of positive integers `nums`, return the maximum possible sum of a strictly ascending contiguous subarray.
hints: Scan through, accumulating a running sum while each element is strictly greater than the previous; reset to just the current element whenever the ascending streak breaks.

title: Count Odd Numbers in an Interval Range
description: Given two non-negative integers `low` and `high`, return the count of odd numbers between `low` and `high` inclusive.
hints: The count of odd numbers up to n is (n + 1) // 2 — subtract that count for (low - 1) from the count for high.

title: Global and Local Inversions
description: Given a permutation `nums` of `0` to `n-1`, a global inversion is a pair `i < j` with `nums[i] > nums[j]`; a local inversion is a global inversion with `j == i + 1`. Return `true` if the number of global inversions equals the number of local inversions.
constraints: nums is a permutation of [0, n-1].
hints: Every local inversion is also a global one, so this is really asking: are there any global inversions that AREN'T local (i.e., between elements more than one apart)?
Check that no element is ever more than 1 position away from its sorted (correct) position — equivalently, |nums[i] - i| <= 1 for every i.

title: Best Sightseeing Pair
description: Given an array of positive integers `values` where `values[i]` is the score of sightseeing spot `i`, the score of a pair `(i, j)` with `i < j` is `values[i] + values[j] + i - j`. Return the maximum such score over all pairs.
hints: Rewrite the score as (values[i] + i) + (values[j] - j). Scan left to right, tracking the best (values[i] + i) seen so far among earlier indices, and combine it with the current (values[j] - j).

title: Circular Array Loop
description: Given a circular array `nums` where a positive value means move that many steps forward and a negative value means move that many steps backward (wrapping around), return `true` if there is a cycle of length > 1 following consistently forward or consistently backward moves (not a single-element self-loop).
hints: From each starting index, use slow/fast pointers (Floyd's cycle detection) following moves in a fixed direction (matching the starting element's sign) — a cycle exists if they meet, as long as the cycle length is more than 1 (not a self-loop).

title: Queue Reconstruction by Height
description: Given `people` where `people[i] = [hi, ki]` (person of height `hi` with exactly `ki` people of height >= `hi` standing in front of them), reconstruct and return the queue as an array of `[h, k]` pairs.
hints: Sort people by height descending, and for equal heights, by k ascending.
Insert each person into the result list at index k — since taller people are already placed, this automatically satisfies their k constraint without disturbing it.

title: Falling Squares
description: Squares are dropped one at a time onto the X-axis, given by `positions` where `positions[i] = [left, sideLength]`. A square lands on top of the tallest existing structure in its x-range, or on the ground if nothing is there. Return an array where the `i`-th value is the height of the tallest structure after the `i`-th square lands.
hints: For each new square, find the maximum height among every previously-dropped square whose x-range overlaps this one's — the new square's base is that maximum, and its top is base + sideLength.
Track the running overall maximum height after each drop.

title: Flip Game
description: You and a friend play a game with a string `currentState` of '+' and '-' characters, taking turns flipping two consecutive '++' into '--'. Return every possible state achievable after exactly one valid move, in any order.
hints: Scan for every position where two consecutive '+' characters occur, and for each, produce the string with that pair flipped to '--'.

title: Complex Number Multiplication
description: Given two strings `num1` and `num2` each representing a complex number in the form `"real+imaginaryi"`, return their product, also formatted as `"real+imaginaryi"`.
constraints: num1 and num2 are valid complex number representations.
hints: Parse each string's real and imaginary parts (split on '+', strip the trailing 'i'), then apply the standard complex multiplication formula: (a+bi)(c+di) = (ac-bd) + (ad+bc)i.

title: Shortest Word Distance III
description: Given an array of strings `wordsDict` and two strings `word1` and `word2` (which may be the SAME word, unlike a typical shortest-distance problem), return the shortest distance between their occurrences in the array.
constraints: word1 and word2 both appear in wordsDict (word1 may equal word2).
hints: If word1 and word2 are different, this is the standard two-pointer tracking approach.
If they're the same word, track only the PREVIOUS occurrence of that word and compare distance to the current occurrence each time it's seen again.

title: Longest Word in Dictionary through Deleting
description: Given a string `s` and a string array `dictionary`, return the longest string in `dictionary` that can be formed by deleting some (possibly zero) characters from `s` (keeping the rest in order). If there is a tie in length, return the lexicographically smallest one; return an empty string if none can be formed.
hints: For each candidate word, check with two pointers whether it's a subsequence of s.
Track the best candidate found so far, preferring longer length, then lexicographically smaller.

title: Fraction to Recurring Decimal
description: Given two integers `numerator` and `denominator`, return the fraction as a string; if the decimal part is repeating, enclose the repeating part in parentheses.
hints: Perform long division: the integer part first, then repeatedly multiply the remainder by 10 to get each decimal digit.
Track the position of each remainder value seen — if a remainder repeats, the decimal digits between its first and second occurrence form the repeating block.

title: Integer to English Words
description: Given a non-negative integer `num`, convert it to its English words representation (e.g. 123 -> "One Hundred Twenty Three").
hints: Break the number into groups of 3 digits (ones, thousands, millions, billions).
Write a helper that converts any 3-digit chunk (0-999) to words, then join each non-zero chunk with its scale word ('Thousand', 'Million', 'Billion').

test_cases.expected_output: Twelve Thousand Three Hundred Forty Five
One Million Two Hundred Thirty Four Thousand Five Hundred Sixty Seven

title: Basic Calculator III
description: Given a string `s` representing an expression with non-negative integers, `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, and parentheses, evaluate and return its value (integer division truncates toward zero).
hints: Use a recursive-descent approach over a shared character iterator: when you hit '(', recurse to evaluate the parenthesized sub-expression (the recursion naturally stops at the matching ')').
Apply '*' and '/' immediately against the top of a value stack (since they bind tighter), and push '+'/'-' terms directly, summing the stack at the end.

title: Longest Valid Parentheses
description: Given a string `s` containing only `(` and `)`, return the length of the longest valid (well-formed) parentheses substring.
hints: Use a stack of indices, seeded with -1 as a base marker. Push the index of every '(' ; on ')', pop, and if the stack becomes empty push the current index as a new base marker, otherwise the current valid length is (current index - new stack top).

title: Non-decreasing Subsequences
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return all non-decreasing subsequences of length at least 2, with no duplicate subsequences (the array may contain duplicate values), in any order.
hints: Backtrack through the array in original order (don't sort — that would break the 'subsequence' meaning), only extending the current path with an element that's >= the path's last element.
At each recursion level, skip a value if it's identical to another value already tried at that SAME level, to avoid duplicate subsequences.

title: Minimum Insertion Steps to Make a String Palindrome
description: Given a string `s`, return the minimum number of characters you must insert to make it a palindrome.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: The answer is the length of s minus the length of its Longest Palindromic Subsequence — every character not part of that subsequence needs a mirrored insertion.

title: Hamming Distance
description: Given two integers `x` and `y`, return the Hamming distance between them — the number of bit positions at which they differ.
hints: XOR the two numbers — the result has a 1 bit exactly where they differ. Count the set bits in that result.

title: Total Hamming Distance
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return the sum of the Hamming distances between every pair of elements in the array.
hints: Consider each of the 32 bit positions independently: if `c` numbers have a 1 there and (n-c) have a 0, that bit contributes c*(n-c) to the total (every 1-0 pair differs at that bit).

title: XOR Queries of a Subarray
description: Given an array `arr` and an array of queries `queries` (each `[left, right]`), return an array where each value is the XOR of all elements in `arr[left..right]` inclusive.
hints: Build a prefix-XOR array where prefix[i] is the XOR of arr[0..i-1].
The XOR of arr[left..right] is prefix[right+1] XOR prefix[left], since XOR-ing prefix[left] twice cancels out everything before 'left'.

title: Decode XORed Array
description: An integer array `arr` (of even-or-odd length, all non-negative) is encoded as `encoded[i] = arr[i] XOR arr[i+1]`. Given `encoded` and `first` (the value of `arr[0]`), return the original array `arr`.
hints: Since arr[i+1] = arr[i] XOR encoded[i], reconstruct the array iteratively starting from 'first'.

title: Find the Original Array of Prefix Xor
description: Given an array `pref` where `pref[i]` is the XOR of `arr[0]` through `arr[i]`, return the original array `arr`.
hints: arr[0] = pref[0]. For i > 0, arr[i] = pref[i] XOR pref[i-1] (since XOR-ing away everything before position i-1 leaves just arr[i]).

title: Bitwise AND of Numbers Range
description: Given two integers `left` and `right`, return the bitwise AND of all numbers in the range `[left, right]` inclusive.
hints: The result keeps only the common binary prefix shared by left and right — any bit that differs somewhere in the range gets ANDed to 0 by some number in between.
Repeatedly right-shift both numbers until they're equal, then shift the common value back left by the same amount.

title: Number of Digit One
description: Given an integer `n`, count the total number of digit `1` appearing in all non-negative integers less than or equal to `n`.
hints: For each digit position (ones, tens, hundreds, ...), count how many numbers up to n have a '1' at that position, using the digit to the left (higher), the digit itself, and the digits to the right (lower) of that position.

title: Integer Break
description: Given an integer `n` (n >= 2), break it into the sum of at least two positive integers, and return the maximum product of those integers.
hints: dp[i] = best product achievable by breaking i.
For each i, try every split point j (1 to i-1): the product is either j * (i - j) directly, or j * dp[i - j] (breaking the remainder further) — take the best over all j.

title: K-th Smallest in Lexicographical Order
description: Given integers `n` and `k`, return the `k`-th smallest integer in the range `[1, n]` when all such integers are sorted lexicographically (as strings).
hints: Think of the numbers as nodes in a 10-ary prefix tree. Starting from the current candidate prefix, count how many numbers in [1, n] share that prefix (its 'subtree' size).
If that count is <= remaining k, skip the whole subtree (move to the next sibling prefix); otherwise descend into the subtree (append a 0 digit) and consume one step of k for the prefix itself.

title: Perfect Rectangle
description: Given an array `rectangles` where `rectangles[i] = [x1, y1, x2, y2]` describes an axis-aligned rectangle, return `true` if they exactly cover a rectangular region without gap or overlap.
hints: The total area of all rectangles must equal the area of their overall bounding box.

Track every corner point with a running XOR-like presence set (toggle membership each time a corner is seen) — at the end, only the 4 corners of the overall bounding box should remain, each seen an odd number of times.

title: Combination Sum IV
description: Given an array of distinct integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the number of possible ORDERED combinations that add up to `target` (different orderings of the same numbers count as distinct combinations).
constraints: All elements of nums are distinct.
hints: dp[t] = number of ordered ways to reach sum t.
For each t from 1 to target, sum dp[t - num] over every num in nums (this naturally counts orderings as distinct, unlike the 'number of combinations' style problems).

title: Out of Boundary Paths
description: Given a grid of size `m x n`, a ball starts at `(startRow, startColumn)` and may move up/down/left/right, up to `maxMove` times. Return the number of ways to move the ball out of the grid boundary, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: dp[moves][r][c] = number of ways to reach out-of-bounds within exactly `moves` further steps, starting at (r, c).
For each move, sum contributions from each of the 4 directions; moving off the grid contributes 1 way directly.

title: Knight Probability in Chessboard
description: On an `n x n` chessboard, a knight starts at `(row, column)` and makes exactly `k` moves, choosing uniformly at random among its (up to 8) valid knight moves each time (even if that would move it off the board, in which case it stops being able to move further). Return the probability that the knight remains on the board after `k` moves.
hints: dp[r][c] = probability of being on the board at (r, c) after the current number of moves.
Each step, spread each cell's probability equally (1/8 each) among its 8 knight-move destinations that remain on the board.

title: Cherry Pickup II
description: Given a `rows x cols` cherry `grid`, two robots start at the top-left and top-right corners. Each step, both robots move simultaneously one row down, each choosing to stay, move left, or move right by one column. Return the maximum cherries collected together (a cell's cherries can only be counted once even if both robots visit it).
hints: Memoize on (row, col1, col2) — the row both robots are on, and their two column positions.
At each row, try all 3x3 combinations of the two robots' next-column moves, adding the current row's cherries (counted once if col1==col2, otherwise both), plus the best result from the next row.

title: Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick
description: Given a wooden stick of length `n` and an array of `cuts` (positions along the stick to cut), where each cut's cost equals the length of the piece being cut at that moment, return the minimum total cost to perform all the cuts in some order.
hints: Add 0 and n as boundary markers and sort all the cut positions.

dp[i][j] = minimum cost to make all cuts strictly between boundary markers i and j; try every cut k between them as the LAST cut in that range, costing (markers[j] - markers[i]) plus the best cost of the two resulting sub-ranges.

title: Guess Number Higher or Lower II
description: You are playing a guessing game against a number picker: you guess a number from `1` to `n`, and if wrong, you're told whether the actual number is higher or lower, and you pay an amount equal to your guess. Return the minimum amount of money needed to guarantee a win, regardless of which number is picked (worst case).
hints: dp[lo][hi] = minimum guaranteed cost to determine any number in [lo, hi].
For each possible first guess x in [lo, hi], the worst case costs x + max(cost of the left remainder, cost of the right remainder) — minimize over every choice of x.

title: Stone Game III
description: Alice and Bob take turns (Alice first) taking 1, 2, or 3 stones from the FRONT of a row `stoneValue`, each maximizing their own total score with optimal play. Return `"Alice"`, `"Bob"`, or `"Tie"` depending on who wins (or if it's a tie).
hints: dp[i] = the best score DIFFERENCE (current player's total minus opponent's total) achievable from stoneValue[i:] onward.
dp[i] = max over taking 1, 2, or 3 stones of (sum of those stones - dp[i + count]).

title: Frog Jump
description: A frog crosses a river by jumping on stones at positions given by sorted array `stones`. Starting on the first stone with a jump size of 1 unit, if its last jump was `k` units, its next jump must be `k-1`, `k`, or `k+1` units (all positive). Return `true` if the frog can reach the last stone.
constraints: stones is sorted in strictly increasing order.
hints: Track, for each stone, the set of jump sizes that could have landed the frog there.
From each stone with an incoming jump size k, try jump sizes k-1, k+1, k to see if they land exactly on another stone in the array.

title: Maximum Length of Repeated Subarray
description: Given two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2`, return the length of the longest common contiguous subarray (a run of consecutive elements appearing in both arrays in the same order).
hints: dp[i][j] = length of the common run ending exactly at nums1[i-1] and nums2[j-1].
dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 if nums1[i-1] == nums2[j-1], else 0 (a mismatch resets the run, unlike the subsequence version).

title: Number of Ways to Form a Target String Given a Dictionary
description: Given a list of equal-length strings `words` and a string `target`, form `target` by choosing characters from `words` in increasing order of column index (each column of `words` may be used at most once overall, but any row within an allowed column). Return the number of ways to form `target`, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
constraints: All words have the same length.
hints: Precompute, for each column position, how many words have each letter there.
dp[i][j] = ways to form target[:i] using the first j columns; either skip column j (dp[i][j-1]) or use it for target[i-1] (dp[i-1][j-1] * count of target[i-1] in column j-1).

title: Minimum Falling Path Sum II
description: Given an `n x n` integer matrix `grid`, return the minimum sum of a falling path, where each step must move to a cell in the next row that is in a DIFFERENT column than the current cell (not just non-diagonal — any different column is allowed).
hints: For each row, you only ever need the smallest and second-smallest values from the previous row (and their column), since the best choice for any current column is the previous row's minimum, unless that minimum was in the same column, in which case use the second-smallest.

title: Distinct Subsequences
description: Given two strings `s` and `t`, return the number of distinct subsequences of `s` that equal `t`.
constraints: s and t consist of English letters.
hints: dp[i][j] = number of ways s[:i] contains t[:j] as a subsequence.
If s[i-1] == t[j-1], dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] (use this match) + dp[i-1][j] (skip it); otherwise dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j].

title: Scramble String
description: A scrambled string is produced by recursively partitioning a string into two non-empty substrings and randomly deciding whether to swap them, applying this recursively. Given two strings `s1` and `s2` of the same length, return `true` if `s2` is a scrambled string of `s1`.
constraints: s1 and s2 consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Recursively try every split point: either both halves match without swapping (s1's prefix matches s2's prefix, and suffixes match), or with swapping (s1's prefix matches s2's SUFFIX of the same length).
A quick character-count mismatch check lets you bail out early before recursing. Memoize on the (s1, s2) pair.

title: Decode Ways II
description: A message of digits and the wildcard `*` (representing any digit 1-9 for a lone position, or any digit 0-9 within a valid pair) is decoded using 'A'=1 .. 'Z'=26. Given a string `s`, return the number of ways to decode it, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: dp[i] = ways to decode s[:i]. For a single character, count how many of its possible digit values (1-9) are valid; for a pair, count how many combinations of both characters' possible digit values fall in 10-26.
Enumerating each '*' character's small set of possible literal digits directly (rather than deriving formulas by hand) keeps the counting unambiguous.

title: 4 Keys Keyboard
description: Imagine a special keyboard with 4 keys: 'A' (types one 'A'), Ctrl-A (select all), Ctrl-C (copy), Ctrl-V (paste, appends the current selection). Given an integer `n` (total number of key presses allowed), return the maximum number of 'A' characters you can display.
hints: dp[i] = max A's achievable with i presses.
Either just press 'A' (dp[i-1] + 1), or, for some earlier point j, press 'A' up to j, then do Ctrl-A/Ctrl-C/Ctrl-V for the remaining (i-j) presses which multiplies dp[j] by (i-j-1) pastes.

title: Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination
description: You are in a city of `n` intersections connected by bidirectional `roads`, each `[u, v, time]`. Return the number of ways to travel from intersection `0` to intersection `n-1` in the minimum possible time, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: Run Dijkstra's algorithm from node 0, and alongside the shortest distance to each node, track the number of distinct shortest paths reaching it.
When relaxing an edge to a strictly shorter distance, overwrite the way-count; when matching the current shortest distance exactly, add to it.

title: Minimum Number of Vertices to Reach All Nodes
description: Given a directed acyclic graph of `n` nodes and `edges`, return the smallest set of vertices such that every node in the graph is reachable from at least one vertex in that set.
hints: In a DAG, a node can only be 'missed' if it has no incoming edge — every node with in-degree 0 MUST be in the answer set, and it can be shown these are also sufficient.

title: Find the City With the Smallest Number of Neighbors at a Threshold Distance
description: Given `n` cities connected by weighted `edges`, and a `distanceThreshold`, find the city that has the smallest number of OTHER cities reachable within `distanceThreshold` (breaking ties by preferring the city with the greatest index). Return that city's index.
hints: Run Floyd-Warshall to get all-pairs shortest distances.
For each city, count how many others are within the threshold; scan cities in increasing index order and keep the best (using <= so a tie updates to the larger index, matching the tie-break rule).

title: Reconstruct Itinerary
description: Given airline tickets as parallel arrays `ticketsFrom` and `ticketsTo` (each index a ticket from one airport to another), reconstruct the itinerary starting from "JFK" that uses every ticket exactly once. If multiple valid itineraries exist, return the lexicographically smallest one (assume a valid itinerary using all tickets always exists).
constraints: All airports are represented by three uppercase English letters.
hints: This is finding an Eulerian path — Hierholzer's algorithm: greedily follow edges (always picking the lexicographically smallest destination available), and when stuck, backtrack, adding the current airport to the front of the route.
A min-heap (or sorted list) of destinations per departure airport gives the lexicographically smallest choice at each step.

title: Employee Free Time
description: Given `schedule`, the combined busy-time intervals of every employee across a company (flattened into a single array of `[start, end]` intervals, order irrelevant), return the list of finite common free time intervals shared by everyone, sorted by start time (ignore the unbounded free time before the first busy interval and after the last).
hints: Sort all the busy intervals by start time and merge every overlapping (or touching) one together.
The free time gaps are exactly the space between the end of one merged interval and the start of the next.

title: Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column
description: Given `stones` where `stones[i] = [xi, yi]`, a stone can be removed if it shares a row or column with another stone that hasn't been removed. Return the maximum number of stones that can be removed.
hints: Union-Find each stone's row and column together (using a shared namespace, e.g. tagging rows and columns distinctly so they don't collide).
Within each connected component, every stone but one can be removed — so the answer is (total stones) minus (number of components).

title: Minimum Time to Collect All Apples in a Tree
description: Given a tree of `n` nodes rooted at `0`, described by `edges`, and `hasApple[i]` indicating whether node `i` has an apple, return the minimum time needed to walk from node 0, collect every apple, and return to node 0 (each edge takes 1 second to cross in each direction).
hints: DFS from the root: a subtree only needs to be visited (costing 2 for the edge down and back) if it contains an apple somewhere within it.

title: All Ancestors of a Node in a Directed Acyclic Graph
description: Given a directed acyclic graph of `n` nodes and `edges`, return, for every node, the sorted list of its ancestors (nodes that can reach it via a directed path).
hints: For each node, DFS forward through the graph, marking every reachable descendant as having this node as an ancestor.

title: Find All People With Secret
description: `n` people (0 to n-1) attend `meetings` (each `[a, b, time]`), where person 0 knows a secret at time 0 and knowing it spreads instantly to anyone else in the same meeting. Given `firstPerson` (the first person person 0 shares the secret with), return every person who ends up knowing the secret, in any order.
hints: Process meetings grouped by time, earliest first. Within each time group, union everyone who meets together.

After processing a time group, any person not connected (via Union-Find) to person 0 at that point should be 'un-shared' — reset their parent to themselves, since secrecy can't have reached them through only same-instant meetings.

title: Checking Existence of Edge Length Limited Paths
description: Given `n` nodes and an undirected weighted `edgeList` (each `[u, v, dis]`), and `queries` (each `[p, q, limit]`), return a boolean array where each value indicates whether there exists a path between `p` and `q` such that every edge on it has a weight strictly less than `limit`.
hints: Process queries offline, sorted by their limit ascending. Also sort edges by weight ascending.

For each query, union every edge with weight strictly less than the query's limit (advancing a pointer through the sorted edge list, never going backward), then just check whether p and q are in the same Union-Find component.

title: Minimum Fuel Cost to Report to the Capital
description: There are `n` cities forming a tree rooted at city 0 (the capital), connected by `roads`. Every city has one representative who must travel to the capital by car (seating `seats` people each, cars can be combined/shared along the way). Return the minimum total fuel needed (1 liter per car per road traveled).
hints: DFS from the capital: each subtree's total number of people traveling through its connecting edge determines how many car-loads (ceil(people / seats)) are needed to cross that one edge.
Sum ceil(subtree size / seats) over every edge.

title: Maximum Subarray Min-Product
description: The min-product of an array is its minimum element multiplied by its sum. Given an array of positive integers `nums`, return the maximum min-product of any non-empty contiguous subarray, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: For each element as the minimum, find how far the subarray can extend left and right while staying >= that element (using a monotonic stack to find the nearest smaller element on each side).
That element's best min-product is itself times the sum of that maximal range; track the overall maximum.

title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
description: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the length of the shortest non-empty contiguous subarray with a sum of at least `k`, or `-1` if none exists.
hints: Build the prefix sum array, then use a monotonic increasing deque of indices into it.

For each new prefix index, pop from the front whenever the sum requirement is satisfied (recording the length), and pop from the back whenever the current prefix is smaller than the back (since a smaller, later prefix is always a better left boundary for future windows).

title: Jump Game VI
description: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, starting at index 0, you may jump to any index within `k` steps forward. Return the maximum score achievable at the last index, where your score is the sum of every `nums` value at the indices you land on (including the start).
hints: dp[i] = best score reaching index i = nums[i] + max(dp[i-k..i-1]).
Maintain that sliding-window maximum with a monotonic decreasing deque of indices for O(n) total time.

title: Minimum Cost to Hire K Workers
description: There are `n` workers with `quality[i]` and minimum acceptable `wage[i]`. When hiring exactly `k` workers, every hired worker must be paid proportionally to their quality (relative to the group), and at least their minimum wage. Return the minimum total cost to hire exactly `k` workers.
hints: Sort workers by their wage-to-quality ratio. For a group paid at a given ratio, the total cost is (ratio * sum of qualities) — so for each worker taken as the group's 'rate-setter' (highest ratio in the group), minimize the summed quality of the k cheapest-quality workers among those with ratio <= this one.
A max-heap of qualities (capped at size k) tracks that minimal sum efficiently as you scan workers in increasing ratio order.

title: Maximum Performance of a Team
description: Given `n` engineers with `speed[i]` and `efficiency[i]`, choose at most `k` engineers to form a team whose performance is (sum of chosen speeds) times (minimum chosen efficiency). Return the maximum performance possible, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: Sort engineers by efficiency descending, so each engineer processed becomes a candidate for 'minimum efficiency in the team' among everyone processed so far.
Keep a min-heap of speeds (capped at size k-1 extra plus the current), tracking a running speed sum, and compute performance = speedSum * currentEfficiency at each step.

title: Minimum Deletions to Make Character Frequencies Unique
description: Given a string `s`, return the minimum number of characters to delete so that no two distinct characters have the same frequency.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Count each character's frequency. Process frequencies from largest to smallest, greedily reducing any frequency that collides with one already claimed (by deleting characters) until it's unique or reaches 0.
Track a set of frequency values already 'claimed' to detect collisions.

title: Partition Array for Maximum Sum
description: Given an integer array `arr` and an integer `k`, partition it into contiguous subarrays of length at most `k`, where each subarray's values are all replaced by that subarray's maximum. Return the largest possible sum of the resulting array.
hints: dp[i] = best sum for the first i elements.
For each i, try every possible length j (1 to k) for the LAST partition ending at i, using the max of that trailing segment times its length, added to dp[i-j].

title: Longest String Chain
description: Given an array of strings `words`, a string chain is a sequence where each word is formed by inserting exactly one letter into the previous word (without reordering the rest). Return the length of the longest possible word chain using words from the array.
constraints: words[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Sort words by length. For each word, try removing each single character to see if the resulting predecessor is also in the word set — if so, this word could extend that predecessor's chain.
dp[word] = 1 + max(dp[predecessor]) over every valid predecessor found this way.

title: Maximum Erasure Value
description: Given an integer array `nums`, erase one contiguous subarray consisting of unique elements to maximize the sum of the removed elements. Return that maximum sum.
hints: Slide a window that always contains only unique values, shrinking from the left whenever a duplicate would be added, tracking a running window sum and the maximum seen.

title: Count Sorted Vowel Strings
description: Given an integer `n`, return the number of strings of length `n` that consist only of vowels (a, e, i, o, u) and are sorted in non-decreasing (lexicographic) order.
hints: dp[i][v] = number of non-decreasing strings of length i ending with vowel v (indexed 0-4).
dp[i][v] = sum of dp[i-1][v'] for every v' <= v; base case dp[1][v] = 1 for every vowel.

title: Number of Sub-arrays With Odd Sum
description: Given an array of integers `arr`, return the number of non-empty contiguous subarrays with an odd sum, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: Track running counts of how many prefix sums so far have been even vs odd.

A subarray ending at the current index has an odd sum exactly when the current prefix parity differs from an earlier prefix's parity — accumulate contributions from the opposite-parity count as you scan.

title: Find Two Non-overlapping Sub-arrays Each With Target Sum
description: Given an array of positive integers `arr` and an integer `target`, find two non-overlapping contiguous subarrays, each summing to exactly `target`, minimizing the sum of their lengths. Return that minimum sum of lengths, or `-1` if no such pair exists.
hints: Slide a window to find every subarray summing to target; track, for each ending position, the shortest such subarray ending at or before that position.
For each subarray found ending at index i, combine its length with the best 'shortest subarray ending before its start' found so far, to get a candidate non-overlapping pair.

title: Longest Happy String
description: A string is happy if it contains no 'aaa', 'bbb', or 'ccc' as a substring. Given integers `a`, `b`, `c` (the maximum number of 'a', 'b', 'c' characters usable), return the longest possible happy string, or an empty string if none can be built with positive length. If multiple answers of maximum length exist, return the one produced by always greedily using the currently most-available letter.
hints: Greedily append whichever remaining letter has the most count available; if that would create a run of 3, use the next-most-available letter instead for this position.
A max-heap of (remaining count, letter) makes this greedy choice efficient.

title: Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards
description: There are `cardPoints[i]` points on card `i`, arranged in a row. In one step you may take a card from the beginning or the end of the row, and you must take exactly `k` cards total. Return the maximum score achievable.
hints: Taking k cards from the ends is equivalent to LEAVING a contiguous window of (n-k) cards in the middle untaken — minimize that window's sum, then subtract it from the total.

title: Minimum Deletions to Make String Balanced
description: Given a string `s` of 'a' and 'b' characters, return the minimum number of deletions so that no 'b' appears before any 'a' in the resulting string.
hints: Scan left to right, tracking the count of 'b' seen so far and the total deletions needed.

At each 'a', either it's fine (if no 'b' precedes any future need) — specifically, take the minimum of (delete this 'a', costing 1) or (it stays, meaning every 'b' seen so far must eventually be deleted) — track deletions as min(deletions + 1, bCount).

title: Maximum Number of Balloons
description: Given a string `text`, return the maximum number of times the word "balloon" can be formed using characters from `text` (each character used at most as many times as it appears).
constraints: text consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Count the letters in text. "balloon" needs 1 'b', 1 'a', 2 'l', 2 'o', 1 'n' — divide each available count by its needed count and take the minimum.

title: Rings and Rods
description: There are 10 rods (labeled 0-9), and rings are added described by string `rings` (pairs of a color character 'R'/'G'/'B' followed by a rod digit). Return the number of rods that have all three colors of rings on them.
hints: Process the string two characters at a time (color, rod), tracking which colors have appeared on each rod (e.g. with a set per rod). Count rods whose set reaches size 3.

title: Find Numbers with Even Number of Digits
description: Given an array of integers `nums`, return how many of them have an even number of digits.
hints: Convert each number to a string and check whether its length is even.

title: How Many Numbers Are Smaller Than the Current Number
description: Given an array `nums`, return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the count of elements smaller than `nums[i]` anywhere in the array.
hints: Sort a copy of the array; the first index at which each value appears in the sorted copy is exactly the count of elements smaller than it.

title: Count Good Triplets
description: Given an array `arr` and integers `a`, `b`, `c`, return the number of triplets `(i, j, k)` with `i < j < k` such that `|arr[i]-arr[j]| <= a`, `|arr[j]-arr[k]| <= b`, and `|arr[i]-arr[k]| <= c`.
hints: The array is small enough to just check every triplet directly with three nested loops.

title: Matrix Block Sum
description: Given an `m x n` matrix `mat` and an integer `k`, return a matrix `answer` where `answer[i][j]` is the sum of every element in `mat` within distance `k` (Chebyshev, both row and column) of `(i, j)`, clipped to the matrix bounds.
hints: Build a 2D prefix sum table first, then each answer cell is a single O(1) rectangle-sum lookup using that table, clipping the query rectangle to the matrix bounds.

title: Minimum Cost to Move Chips to the Same Position
description: Given `position[i]`, the position of the `i`-th chip, you may move any chip by 2 positions for free, or by 1 position for a cost of 1. Return the minimum total cost to move all chips to the same position.
hints: Moving by 2 is free, so every chip can reach either position 0 or position 1 for free (depending on its parity).
The answer is just the smaller of (count of chips at even positions) and (count of chips at odd positions) — move the minority group by 1 to join the majority.

title: Find Lucky Integer in an Array
description: A lucky integer is one whose value equals its own frequency in the array. Given an array of integers `arr`, return the largest lucky integer, or `-1` if none exists.
hints: Count the frequency of every value, then check which values equal their own count, taking the largest such value.

title: Count Largest Group
description: For every integer from `1` to `n`, group it by the sum of its digits. Return the number of groups that have the largest size.
hints: Compute the digit sum of every number from 1 to n, tally group sizes, then count how many groups share the maximum size.

title: Sum of Unique Elements
description: Given an integer array `nums`, return the sum of every element that appears exactly once in the array.
hints: Count the frequency of each value, then sum only the values whose count is exactly 1.

title: Decompress Run-Length Encoded List
description: Given a run-length encoded list `nums` where each consecutive pair `[freq, val]` means `val` repeated `freq` times, return the fully decompressed array.
hints: Walk through the array two elements at a time, appending the value that many times to the result.

title: Create Target Array in the Given Order
description: Given arrays `nums` and `index` of the same length, build a target array by inserting `nums[i]` at position `index[i]` (shifting later elements right), processing i from 0 to n-1. Return the resulting target array.
hints: Simulate directly: maintain a list and use its insert-at-index operation for each (nums[i], index[i]) pair in order.

title: Maximum Nesting Depth of the Parentheses
description: Given a valid parentheses string `s` (which may also contain other characters), return the maximum nesting depth of the parentheses.
constraints: s consists of digits, English letters, and the characters '(', ')', '+', '-', '*', '/'.
hints: Track a running depth counter: increment on '(', decrement on ')', and record the maximum value reached.

title: Goal Parser Interpretation
description: Given a string `command` consisting of "G", "()", and "(al)", interpret it: "G" stays "G", "()" becomes "o", and "(al)" becomes "al". Return the resulting interpreted string.
hints: Scan the string once: on 'G' emit 'G'; on '(' check whether the very next character is ')' (emit 'o') or 'a' (emit 'al', skipping to the matching ')').

title: Truncate Sentence
description: Given a sentence `s` (words separated by single spaces, no leading/trailing spaces) and an integer `k`, return the sentence truncated to its first `k` words.
constraints: k is in the range [1, number of words in s].
hints: Split the sentence on spaces, take the first k words, and rejoin them with single spaces.

inputs.s: What is the solution to this problem

title: Count the Number of Consistent Strings
description: Given a string `allowed` of distinct characters and an array of strings `words`, return the number of strings in `words` that consist ONLY of characters from `allowed` (each word may reuse characters as needed).
hints: Put the allowed characters in a set, then for each word check that every one of its characters is a member of that set.

title: Minimum Changes to Make Alternating Binary String
description: Given a binary string `s`, return the minimum number of character flips needed so that no two adjacent characters are equal.
hints: There are only two possible target alternating patterns (starting with '0' or starting with '1'). Count mismatches against each, and take the smaller count.
